evals.prompt: Sanity-check me before I take this to our CFO on Thursday. Brightpath Analytics, we sell a $38,000 ACV analytics platform, 74% gross margin, and our direct CAC is $9,500. We have a reseller called Calderon Systems on the table at a 30% discount off list, and their plan says 12 closed deals in year two. To acquire those 12 we would spend $24,000 MDF, about 0.3 of a partner manager which is $39,000 loaded, $15,000 of enablement and certification delivery, $9,000 of extra support load, and $2,000 of portal allocation. That is roughly $7,400 a head against our $9,500 direct CAC, so a 22% acquisition win. Am I reading that right?
evals.expected_output: A partner economics analysis that rejects the per-customer CAC comparison, restates both sides as acquisition cost per $1 of net revenue, finds the partner more expensive than direct rather than 22% cheaper, and lands on renegotiate or do-not-sign at 30%.
expectations: Rejects the per-customer comparison of roughly $7,400 against $9,500 as invalid, because the 30% discount lowers revenue per partner deal so the two figures price different goods
States net revenue per partner deal as $26,600, being $38,000 less the 30% discount
States year-two partner net revenue as $319,200 and the discount value conceded as $136,800
Expresses direct acquisition cost as $0.25 per $1 of net revenue, from $9,500 on a $38,000 ACV
Expresses partner acquisition cost per $1 of net revenue using the $89,000 of non-discount cost over $319,200 of net revenue, landing between $0.27 and $0.29
Concludes the partner is more expensive per $1 of net revenue than the direct motion, reversing the user's claimed 22% win

Names which costing convention it used - revenue booked gross with the discount charged to acquisition cost, or revenue booked net of discount with the discount excluded - and does not mix the two inside one comparison
Does not declare one of the two costing conventions more correct, more conservative, or preferred over the other
States the go/no-go threshold the model is judged against before delivering any verdict
Addresses incrementality explicitly rather than assuming every Calderon deal is net-new
Reports a sensitivity pass naming which assumptions flip the verdict, with effective discount among them
Delivers a renegotiate or do-not-sign verdict at 30%, naming the discount level or deal count that would clear the direct benchmark, instead of recommending signature on the user's figures

evals.prompt: Quick one. Halverson Group is our best reseller - they closed $2.4M of list ACV for us last year at a 22% discount. Our average deal is $60K, gross margin is 68%, and customers stick around about five years, so partner LTV is $300K a head. On top of the discount we pay them $180,000 MDF, and internally they cost us one full-time partner manager at $140,000, $70,000 of certification delivery and $40,000 of extra support. I want to put 'Halverson contributed $2.4M and each customer is worth $300K' in the Q1 partner review. Anything wrong with that?
evals.expected_output: A restatement that strips the headline revenue down to net contribution across the full cost stack, recomputes lifetime value on gross margin instead of revenue, and challenges the asserted five-year lifetime.
expectations: Refuses to report $2.4M as Halverson's contribution and restates it net of the full partner cost stack
Names every cost bucket in the restatement: the 22% discount, the $180,000 MDF, the $140,000 of partner-manager time, the $70,000 of certification delivery and the $40,000 support uplift
States the 22% discount in money as $528,000
Reports total partner cost of $958,000 against the $2.4M headline
Reports restated revenue net of partner cost below $1.5M rather than $2.4M
Rejects the $300,000 lifetime value because it is computed on revenue rather than on gross margin
Recomputes lifetime value on the 68% gross margin, giving roughly $204,000 per customer on the stated five-year assumption
Applies gross margin once, not twice, in the lifetime-value calculation
Flags the five-year lifetime as asserted with no churn basis behind it
Asks the user for the churn rate or a measured average customer lifetime for this segment instead of substituting an assumed figure
Separates partner-sourced from partner-influenced revenue, or asks which share of the $2.4M is which, instead of accepting one blended attributed number
States that the review should carry annual net contribution rather than headline revenue, and lists what remains unverified in the supplied figures

evals.prompt: I am building the board deck for our channel program review next month. Opening slide I want three stats I pulled off a channel blog: 80% of channel revenue comes from the top 20% of partners, only 11% of partners hit their incentive goals, and most partners never transact at all. Then the ask: we have 140 signed partners, 19 of them closed anything last year, and I want approval to cut the bottom 40 by tenure - anyone signed more than three years ago with under $50K. Help me tighten the argument.
evals.expected_output: A rewrite of the board slide that refuses all three untraceable statistics, substitutes attributable figures with their evidence class, and replaces tenure-based pruning with net contribution.
expectations: Flags the 80/20 channel-revenue concentration figure as untraceable and refuses to present it as fact
Flags the 11% incentive-attainment figure as untraceable and refuses to present it as fact
Flags 'most partners never transact' as untraceable, noting that the circulating variants trace to no original study
Offers the Forrester 2016 finding that 14% of channel incentives meet their goals as the attributable substitute, labeled as an analyst survey

Offers the CRN Research 2025 Partner Journey Study figure - 70% of partners terminated or dormant within twelve months, split 29% terminated and 41% stopped selling - as the best-attributed adjacent number
Attaches an evidence class to every benchmark it allows into the deck
States that the direction of heavy partner concentration is credible even though the specific 80/20 figure is not
Rejects tenure as the pruning criterion and replaces it with net contribution per partner
States that 140 signed partners with 19 active is a 19-partner channel
Computes or requests revenue per partner on the active count only, warning that dividing by all 140 flatters the program
Requires each partner proposed for cutting to carry a fully-loaded cost-to-serve figure, not just its revenue
Does not invent a replacement statistic where no attributable source exists, writing unverified instead
Notes that a partner below $50K may still be net-contribution positive if it costs almost nothing to serve

evals.prompt: Tessura has been our AWS Marketplace co-sell partner for two years. Last year our CRM shows $3.1M of Tessura-attributed closed-won. My CFO does not believe it is real revenue and wants proof before we renew. My plan is to pause the whole Tessura motion for a quarter, watch what happens to bookings, and bring him the number. Our agreement with them runs 12 months more with EMEA exclusivity and a $750,000 annual minimum we owe them. How would you design the test?
evals.expected_output: An incrementality plan that starts from an assumed-rate band rather than the proposed pause, deletes the pause outright on contractual grounds, and ranks the remaining measurement options by evidence bought per unit of effort.
expectations: Separates attributed revenue from incremental revenue rather than treating the $3.1M as the quantity in question
Cites Blake, Nosko and Tadelis (2015, Econometrica) and the eBay result that 99.5% of brand-keyword clicks were retained after paid search was halted
Does not open by endorsing the channel pause the user proposed
Recommends the assumed-rate band as the first step, stating the assumed incrementality rate as a named assumption
Shows the verdict at 100%, 70% and 40% incremental rather than at a single assumed rate
States that buying an experiment is justified only when the verdict flips inside the plausible range
Deletes the channel pause from the menu outright rather than ranking it last, because suspending the motion would breach the EMEA exclusivity and the $750,000 annual minimum
Names the specific contract terms that killed the pause, recording it as deleted rather than merely unattractive
Ranks the remaining options with the assumed-rate band ahead of matched holdout, and matched holdout ahead of geo split, on evidence bought per unit of effort
States that matched holdout and assumed-rate band carry no compliance cost because both run inside the vendor's own systems
Notes that a geo split amends the rules of engagement and is visible to the partner
States that the academic literature on channel incrementality versus cannibalization is unsettled, documenting both synergy and substitution
Reports the incrementality estimate with its evidence class rather than as a bare percentage

evals.prompt: Setting a ceiling on what we can pay a referral partner per closed customer. Lifetime revenue per customer is $2,400, gross margin 65%, and our target CAC is $350. A partner is asking for $900 per closed customer, one time. Separately our affiliate platform rep told us SaaS programs pay 20-30% recurring, so he thinks $720 is the safe number. What is our actual ceiling and do we take the $900?
evals.expected_output: A ceiling of $1,210 computed from lifetime revenue rather than margin-adjusted LTV, approval of the $900 ask, and the platform rep's benchmark demoted to a labeled vendor figure that does not bind the decision.
expectations: Computes the maximum affordable payout per customer as lifetime revenue multiplied by gross margin, minus target CAC
Uses the $2,400 lifetime revenue figure as the input, not a margin-adjusted lifetime value
Reports a ceiling of $1,210
Does not apply the 65% gross margin twice, and does not report a ceiling near $664
Approves the $900 ask as sitting below the ceiling
States the headroom between the $900 ask and the $1,210 ceiling as $310
Labels the 20-30% recurring SaaS affiliate range as a vendor benchmark supplied by an affiliate platform, not as a constraint on this decision
States that the ceiling, not the platform rep's benchmark, is what binds the payout
Explains that any payout above the ceiling buys revenue at a loss
Names what would move the ceiling: a change in lifetime revenue, in gross margin, or in the target CAC
Asks whether the $2,400 lifetime revenue figure is measured or assumed rather than treating it as verified

evals.prompt: We are a B2B SaaS company - project management for construction firms, $9,600 average annual contract - running a 25% recurring revenue-share affiliate program with 4,100 signed affiliates. Priya Raghunathan, a construction-tech newsletter writer, drove $310,000 of tracked revenue last year on her own. She is asking for a custom 35% rate. Our next two biggest earners are a SaaS coupon site and a cashback browser extension. Build me the economics on whether to give Priya 35%, and while you are at it I would like a P&L for each of the 4,100 so I can see who else deserves a bump.
evals.expected_output: An individually modeled case for the head affiliate on effective rather than stated rev-share, cohort-level treatment of the 4,100-partner tail, and segment-level incrementality that isolates the coupon and cashback partners.
expectations: Models the payout on an effective revenue-share rate rather than on the stated 25% or requested 35% headline rate

States that effective revenue share typically runs 20-40% below the stated rate after refunds, chargebacks, fraud reversals and non-qualifying actions, and labels that range as vendor or practitioner class
Refuses to build 4,100 individual partner P&Ls and models the long tail at cohort level instead
Models Priya individually, treating the head of the distribution the way a B2B reseller would be modeled
Uses B2C per-action mechanics even though the product is sold to businesses, on the grounds that the money flow rather than the buyer decides the model
Does not apply a 6-12 month ramp or a double-cost enablement period to the affiliate motion
Estimates incrementality separately for the coupon site and the cashback extension rather than for the program as a whole
Identifies coupon and cashback partners as the textbook case of attributed but non-incremental volume
Builds a cost stack that still includes tracking or platform fees, fraud losses, payment costs, creative production and program-management time
Computes lifetime value on gross margin, and asks for the gross margin and churn figures that the prompt does not supply
Reports what Priya's $310,000 of tracked revenue becomes once the effective rate and validation deductions are applied, instead of carrying the tracked figure into the verdict unadjusted
States the threshold the 35% decision is judged against before recommending for or against it
Reports the incrementality assumption behind Priya's own traffic with its evidence class rather than assuming her tracked revenue is fully incremental

evals.prompt: We sell a $120,000 list-price industrial IoT platform direct in North America, 71% gross margin, direct CAC around $26,000. To open LATAM we are being pitched a two-tier structure: regional distributor Caravela takes 12% of whatever the resellers pay them, and the resellers under Caravela buy at 30% off our list. Our VP Sales says it is a 30% discount, the distributor's cut comes out of the reseller's side, so nothing changes for us. Model it.
evals.expected_output: A full end-to-end stack model showing the vendor nets roughly $73,920 rather than $84,000, naming double marginalization as the cause and the two-part tariff as the fix, with the channel-mode question raised before the economics settle it.
expectations: Rejects the claim that the distributor's cut comes out of the reseller's side at no cost to the vendor
Models the full two-tier stack end to end rather than one tier at a time
States the net price the vendor actually receives per unit as roughly $73,920 against the $120,000 list
States the effective all-in discount as roughly 38%, not the 30% quoted by the VP Sales
Names double marginalization, and Spengler's 1950 work, as the root cause of margin stacking
Offers the two-part tariff as the peer-reviewed coordination fix, citing Jeuland and Shugan (1983) or McGuire and Staelin (1983)
Labels the 8-15% distributor margin range and the 25-35% VAR gross margin range as vendor or practitioner class, not as settled benchmarks
Compares acquisition cost per $1 of net revenue against the direct motion rather than comparing per-customer figures
Raises whether a partner channel is the right mode for LATAM entry at all before the unit economics settle it, referencing ally-versus-acquire or the transaction-cost make-versus-buy test
Builds a cost-to-serve stack for the LATAM motion that goes beyond the discount alone
Asks for the deal volume, ramp expectation and contract terms the model needs rather than assuming them
Runs a sensitivity pass naming which assumptions flip the LATAM verdict

evals.prompt: Board meeting in nine days and I need a recommendation. Our reseller Oakhurst Technologies is up for renewal at their current 35% discount and I want to push them to 28%. Two complications: Oakhurst has told me twice they will not open their own books to us, and I have no finance analyst free this quarter, so it is me alone on this. None of their deals route through a marketplace - everything is a direct paper contract. What is the right way to build this?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation of the vendor-side contribution model, with the dual-sided P&L and the marketplace-mechanics layer deleted and recorded as deleted with their reasons, plus a named limitation about arguing a split from one ledger.
expectations: Deletes the dual-sided partner P&L from the options rather than listing and demoting it, because Oakhurst will not disclose its own numbers
States the second independent reason the dual-sided model is gone: no finance reviewer is assigned
Deletes the marketplace-mechanics layer because no deal routes through a marketplace
Records each deleted option as deleted and why, so it does not return as scope at a later review
Recommends the vendor-side contribution model as the approach that survives the stated constraints
States that the decision at stake is the split rather than the signature, which would ordinarily promote the dual-sided P&L
Names the resulting limitation: the split cannot be argued honestly from the vendor's ledger alone
Rules out any incrementality experiment on the nine-day timeline and does not propose a matched holdout, a geo split or a channel pause
Recommends the assumed-rate band for incrementality as the only option that fits inside nine days
Asks its clarifying questions one at a time rather than batching them into a single list
Asks for the current direct CAC and the average deal size it buys, without which there is no threshold to test
Asks for product gross margin and churn or average customer lifetime before computing any lifetime value
Fixes the go/no-go threshold for the 28% ask before computing anything

evals.prompt: Enterprise prospect Kessler Freight wants to buy our platform through AWS Marketplace so it retires their EDP commit - $1.8M over three years, as a private offer. Our AE's framing: the marketplace costs us 3%, the customer gets their committed spend burned down so it is basically free money for them, and sales wants an 18% discount on top to get it signed this quarter. One wrinkle, the AWS partner rep asked whether we are hosted entirely on AWS. Our data plane is on AWS but our control plane runs on GCP. Model this deal for me.
evals.expected_output: A routed-deal cost stack in which the 18% win discount dwarfs the marketplace fee, the commit-drawdown 'free money' framing is refused, and the split-plane architecture is flagged against the eligibility restriction.
expectations: Models the 18% win discount and the marketplace fee inside one cost stack rather than treating the fee as the cost of the marketplace route
States the 18% discount as roughly $324,000 against a marketplace fee of roughly $54,000 or less, so the discount dwarfs the fee
Uses the 1.5-3% private-offer fee band rather than assuming the roughly 3% public SaaS listing rate applies
Labels the marketplace fee figures as platform or vendor documentation, the best-attributed class in this domain, and says to verify the current published schedule before quoting it
Rejects the 'free money' framing of commit drawdown
Explains that a qualifying marketplace purchase retires commit at full price, while direct consumption of the same value would cost the buyer less after a negotiated discount
Flags the eligibility risk created by the split architecture: commit retirement was restricted to SaaS hosted entirely on AWS effective May 2025
States that eligibility must be confirmed for this specific product rather than assumed for the SaaS category
Identifies the control plane running on GCP as exactly the configuration that strands commit-retirement eligibility
States that marketplace mechanics settle only the routed-deal cost stack and are a layer on top of a vendor-side contribution model, never a substitute for one
Computes acquisition cost per $1 of net revenue for this routed deal rather than reporting a per-customer figure
Names what happens to the deal thesis if commit retirement turns out to be ineligible, since the buyer's entire motive disappears
Lists open questions covering the unverified fee schedule and the unconfirmed eligibility ruling

evals.prompt: Nine months ago we signed Vantree, an MSP, on the back of a business case I built. Modeled partner CAC was $6,200; actuals say $9,800. Direct CAC is $8,400. Vantree-sourced customers are churning at 19% annually against 7% for our direct-sourced base. Our CRO says MSP relationships take 18 months and we should give it more time - we have also sunk about $210,000 into enabling them. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: A diagnostic worked in cheapest-first order on the CAC overrun, a retention-gap read against the practitioner threshold and the survey figure, an assumption audit, and a prune-or-continue call made on net contribution rather than tenure or sunk cost.
expectations: Works the partner-CAC-exceeds-direct diagnostic in a stated order, cheapest cause first
Checks attribution double-counting of influenced deals first, as a re-run of the query at near-zero effort
Checks the commission or discount rate against deal size second, as roughly an hour of arithmetic against a term that can be renegotiated
Checks partner lead quality last, as the slowest fix, needing cohort win-rate and retention data
Identifies the 12 percentage point retention gap between 19% and 7% as beyond the 10-15pp practitioner threshold that signals ICP misalignment
Cites the SaaS Capital survey of August 2019 finding channel-majority companies running roughly 3pp lower retention, showing how far outside survey-typical this gap sits
Labels the 10-15pp threshold as a practitioner rule of thumb rather than a measured standard
Recomputes lifetime value on the 19% partner-sourced churn rather than on the direct-cohort figure used in the original model
Rejects the $210,000 of sunk enablement spend as a reason to continue
Rejects tenure and the CRO's 18-month convention as the decision basis, and prunes or continues on net contribution
Runs an assumption audit naming which modeled inputs proved wrong and by how much, as the input to the next model
Distinguishes judging the original economic decision from running Vantree's ongoing performance scorecard, and points the ongoing scorecard at the partner performance review discipline
Compares realized partner CAC of $9,800 against both the $6,200 projection and the $8,400 direct figure on a like-for-like basis rather than per customer alone
